summary:
Orbiting Worlds is a 3D browser game that teaches how real science missions are designed, from the first idea all the way to operations in space. The player is a mission systems engineer who lives in a cozy base with a space pet. They take four missions through the six stages of mission design: a yeast experiment on the ISS, a constellation that watches the Sun, a satellite fleet mapping Earth's magnetosphere, and a sample return from Phobos. Every choice costs budget, time, mass or risk, so players learn trade offs and margins by doing instead of by answering quizzes. On expeditions to the Moon, Mars and Earth, players walk around tiny planets and collect real samples and instruments.

We want systems engineering to feel approachable and fun for students who would never open a technical manual, and we want to show them that failure is part of learning.

We built the game with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, made the 3D models and scenes with Three.js, added sound with WebAudio, and used Claude to help us debug. We also thought about accessibility, offline play, how well it runs on ordinary laptops, scientific accuracy, and keeping it unofficial with no NASA logos.
details:
**What does your project do, and how does it work?**

*Orbiting Worlds* is a 3D browser game that simulates end-to-end space mission design, from initial concept to orbital operations. Playing as a mission systems engineer inside a first-person habitat, users guide four missions (an ISS yeast nutrient experiment, a solar-monitoring constellation, a magnetosphere-mapping satellite fleet, and a Phobos sample return) through six core engineering phases: identifying needs, developing concepts, defining requirements, designing, testing, and operating. Every choice dynamically impacts live budget, schedule, mass, power, and risk margins, while surface expeditions on Earth, the Moon, and Mars let players collect real planetary samples and operate field instruments.

**What benefits does it have?**

The game promotes experiential learning by replacing traditional quizzes with interactive simulations and open-ended engineering trade-offs that have no single correct answer. When designs fail, the system provides immediate, constructive feedback that diagnoses the exact technical error and allows instant retries. Furthermore, the entire application runs offline as a self-contained single file, ensuring broad accessibility without installation barriers.

**What is the intended impact?**

*Orbiting Worlds* aims to demystify systems engineering for students who might otherwise avoid dense technical manuals. By working backward from scientific objectives, players learn why technical margins matter and why every requirement must be validated, ultimately sparking curiosity in space science and aerospace careers.

**What tools did you use?**

The game was built using standard web technologies (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript), alongside Three.js for rendering 3D models, planets, and scenes, and the Web Audio API for procedural sound effects and music. We also utilized Claude to assist with debugging during development.

**What factors did your team consider?**

Our team prioritized scientific accuracy by modeling instruments, samples, and mission architectures after real-world spaceflight programs while strictly avoiding official agency logos or trademarked assets. We also focused on accessibility and performance, optimizing the 3D engine to run smoothly on standard laptops and packaging the game for offline play so educational rigor never comes at the expense of smooth, engaging gameplay.
